noteBlocks.lede: $\dfrac{6}{8}$ cancels to $\dfrac{3}{4}$ because 2 divides the whole of the top and the whole of the bottom. Algebraic fractions obey the same rule, and the catch is that you cannot see the factors until you have factorised. So factorising is always the first move.
can: Cancel whole factors only, top and bottom.
Factorise a quadratic numerator and denominator before cancelling.
Turn a division into a multiplication by flipping the second fraction.

noteBlocks.text: Simplifying, multiplying and dividing algebraic fractions

noteBlocks.md: This is the topic that separates the top grades, and there is one rule in it: **you may only cancel a factor of the whole top with a factor of the whole bottom**. The factors therefore have to be visible before anything is crossed out, which turns every question here into a factorising question first.

noteBlocks.text: Why factorising has to come first

noteBlocks.md:
Cancelling is division. $\dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{2 \times 3}{2 \times 4} = \dfrac{3}{4}$ works because 2 divides the **whole** top and the **whole** bottom. Now look at $\dfrac{2 + 3}{2 + 4}$: that is $\dfrac{5}{6}$, and no crossing out is allowed, because the 2s are parts of sums.
Algebra behaves the same way.

noteBlocks.prompt: In $\dfrac{2 + 3}{2 + 4}$, may the two 2s be cancelled?
options: No, they are parts of sums
noteBlocks.answer: No, they are parts of sums
noteBlocks.explain: $\dfrac{2 + 3}{2 + 4} = \dfrac{5}{6}$, and cancelling would give $\dfrac{3}{4}$. Only a factor of the whole top and bottom may go.

noteBlocks.md:
$\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + 7x + 12}$: as written, nothing cancels. Factorise both parts and a common bracket appears:
$\dfrac{(x + 3)(x - 3)}{(x + 3)(x + 4)} = \dfrac{x - 3}{x + 4}$.
If you ever doubt an answer here, substitute. At $x = 1$ the original is $\dfrac{-8}{20} = -0.4$, and so is $\dfrac{-2}{5}$. Crossing out the $x^2$ terms instead would give $\dfrac{-9}{7x + 12}$, which is $-0.47\ldots$ at $x = 1$ — a different expression.

noteBlocks.title: November 2024 M4 Q19
noteBlocks.md: About a third got full marks. Most took the common factor out, though some divided by it instead of factorising. Weaker candidates cancelled single terms across the fraction, or tried to solve the expression as though it were an equation.

options: Factorise the top and the bottom
noteBlocks.answer: Factorise the top and the bottom
noteBlocks.explain: Nothing may be cancelled while either part is still a sum.

noteBlocks.md:
When there are no brackets, it is ordinary index work. Deal with the numbers and the letters separately:
$\dfrac{6x^2}{8x} = \dfrac{3x}{4}$, because $\dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$ and $\dfrac{x^2}{x} = x^{2-1} = x$.
To multiply, tops times tops and bottoms times bottoms, and indices **add**:
$\dfrac{2x^2}{3} \times \dfrac{x}{6} = \dfrac{2x^3}{18} = \dfrac{x^3}{9}$.
Cancelling before you multiply keeps the numbers small and is usually quicker.

Every question here is a factorising question in disguise. Four tools cover all of them:
**A common factor.** $2x + 10 = 2(x + 5)$, and $3x^2 - 27 = 3(x^2 - 9)$ — then look again, because that bracket factorises too.
**The difference of two squares.** $x^2 - 25 = (x + 5)(x - 5)$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of the four tools factorises $x^2 - 25$?
noteBlocks.explain: Two terms, both squares, a minus between: $(x + 5)(x - 5)$.

noteBlocks.md:
**A quadratic $x^2 + bx + c$.** Two numbers multiplying to $c$ and adding to $b$.
**Grouping**, when the numerator has four terms: $ab + 3a + 2b + 6 = a(b + 3) + 2(b + 3) = (a + 2)(b + 3)$.
So $\dfrac{2x + 10}{x^2 - 25} = \dfrac{2(x + 5)}{(x + 5)(x - 5)} = \dfrac{2}{x - 5}$.

$\dfrac{25 - w^2}{w^2 - 3w - 10}$. Factorise in the order given: $25 - w^2 = (5 + w)(5 - w)$, and $w^2 - 3w - 10 = (w - 5)(w + 2)$.
The top has $(5 - w)$ and the bottom has $(w - 5)$. They are not identical, but they differ only by a sign: $(5 - w) = -(w - 5)$. Pull the minus out and they cancel:
$\dfrac{(5 + w) \times -(w - 5)}{(w - 5)(w + 2)} = -\dfrac{5 + w}{w + 2}$.
Writing the top as $(w + 5)(w - 5)$ instead would lose that minus sign and the whole answer would be the negative of the right one.

noteBlocks.explain: Reversing a subtraction changes the sign of the whole bracket.

noteBlocks.md: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal — and it is the **second** fraction that turns over. After that it is a multiplication, so all the same rules apply.

noteBlocks.md:
$\dfrac{x^2 - 16}{3x} \div \dfrac{x + 4}{6x^2}$
1 Flip: $\dfrac{x^2 - 16}{3x} \times \dfrac{6x^2}{x + 4}$
2 Factorise: $\dfrac{(x + 4)(x - 4)}{3x} \times \dfrac{6x^2}{x + 4}$
3 Cancel: $(x + 4)$ goes, and $\dfrac{6x^2}{3x} = 2x$
4 Finish: $2x(x - 4)$
Notice that no denominator survives, so the answer is not a fraction at all. That is fine.

noteBlocks.explain: Flip and multiply; the $(x + 2)$ brackets cancel.

noteBlocks.title: Why flipping the second fraction works
noteBlocks.md: Dividing by $\dfrac{3}{4}$ asks how many three-quarters fit into the amount, which is the same as taking four thirds of it. A reciprocal is what a fraction must be multiplied by to give 1, so it undoes the division.

$\dfrac{x + 3}{x - 2}$ is a complete answer. Adding '$= 0$', or offering $x = -3$, answers a question nobody asked and can cost the accuracy mark. An expression is simplified; only an equation is solved.
One more habit: leave the answer in brackets. $\dfrac{3(x + 3)}{x + 5}$ is better than $\dfrac{3x + 9}{x + 5}$, because the brackets show that nothing further cancels.

Factorise before anything is cancelled.
Cancel whole brackets only, never single terms.
Flip the second fraction to turn division into multiplication.

Short here at one to three marks, and one of the last questions in M4. Marks are given per factorisation, so write every factorisation down even if the cancelling then defeats you; in a division the flip is a mark on its own. The last mark is the single fraction in lowest terms, left in brackets. Stuck: follow the fixed order — flip, factorise, cancel — and do not improvise.

steps.working: Nothing cancels yet. Factorise the top: $x^2 - 9$ is a difference of two squares, so it is $(x + 3)(x - 3)$.
steps.decision: A fraction only cancels when top and bottom are written as **products**. As sums, $x^2 - 9$ and $x^2 + 7x + 12$ share nothing that can be crossed out.

options: Because cancelling divides, and you can only divide out a factor of the whole top and the whole bottom
Because the $x^2$ terms are not exactly the same
Because the bottom has three terms and the top has two
whyMenu.explain: $\dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{2 \times 3}{2 \times 4}$ cancels because 2 is a factor of both; $\dfrac{2 + 3}{2 + 4}$ does not cancel at all.

steps.working: Factorise the bottom: two numbers multiplying to 12 and adding to 7 are 3 and 4, so $x^2 + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)$.
steps.decision: Both parts get factorised before anything else happens. Doing one and stopping leaves nothing to compare.

steps.working: $\dfrac{(x + 3)(x - 3)}{(x + 3)(x + 4)}$ — the bracket $(x + 3)$ appears in both, so it divides out.
steps.decision: Cancel the whole bracket, not part of it. What remains is a single fraction with no common factor left.
Check that nothing else cancels: $(x - 3)$ and $(x + 4)$ are different brackets, so this is fully simplified. Leave it as brackets rather than expanding.

steps.working: $\dfrac{6x^2}{8x}$: the numbers share a factor of 2, so $\dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{3}{4}$. The letters divide by subtracting indices: $\dfrac{x^2}{x} = x$.
steps.decision: Numbers and letters are handled separately. Dividing powers of the same letter **subtracts** the indices; it never divides them.

whyMenu.explain: $x^2 = x \times x$, and one of them cancels with the single $x$ below.

steps.decision: Both parts simplified. There is no bracket here, so it is ordinary index work, not factorising.
To multiply, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms: $\frac{a}{b} \times \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ac}{bd}$. Multiplying powers of the same letter **adds** the indices.
Simplify at the end: 2 divides into 18 nine times. Cancelling before multiplying would have worked too and kept the numbers smaller.

steps.decision: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal: turn the **second** fraction upside down and change the sign to a multiplication. The first fraction is untouched.
Now factorise everything that will factorise. This is the step most candidates never reach, and it is where the question is actually won.
Cancel across the multiplication: any bracket on a top may cancel with the same bracket on a bottom, and the numbers and powers simplify as usual.

options: Because in a product of fractions every top is multiplied by every top, so a common factor anywhere cancels
Because $(x + 4)$ appears twice, so it becomes $(x+4)^2$
Because only the first fraction may be cancelled
whyMenu.explain: The whole thing is one fraction, $\dfrac{(x+4)(x-4) \times 6x^2}{3x(x+4)}$, so any matching factor divides out.

steps.decision: There is no denominator left, so the answer is a product rather than a fraction. Leaving it factorised is fine; $2x^2 - 8x$ is equally acceptable.

steps.working: Top: $25 - w^2$ is a difference of two squares with the **number first**, so it is $(5 + w)(5 - w)$.
steps.decision: Keep the order the question wrote. $(w + 5)(w - 5)$ would be $w^2 - 25$, the negative of the top, and the answer would come out with the wrong sign.

options: $(w + 5)(w - 5) = w^2 - 25$, which is not the top
The order never matters in a factorisation
whyMenu.explain: Swapping the terms multiplies the whole expression by $-1$.

steps.working: Bottom: two numbers multiplying to $-10$ and adding to $-3$ are $-5$ and $2$, so $w^2 - 3w - 10 = (w - 5)(w + 2)$.
steps.decision: Ordinary quadratic factorising. Now compare: the top has $(5 - w)$ and the bottom has $(w - 5)$ — not identical, but very nearly.
Two brackets that are reverses of each other differ by a factor of $-1$. Pulling the minus sign out makes them identical, and then they cancel.
The minus stays with the fraction. Writing $\dfrac{-(w + 5)}{w + 2}$ or $\dfrac{-w - 5}{w + 2}$ says the same thing.

parts.stem:
Ronan simplifies $\dfrac{x^2 + 5x + 6}{x^2 - 4}$ by crossing out the $x^2$ on the top and the $x^2$ on the bottom, giving $\dfrac{5x + 6}{-4}$.

Explain why this is not correct.

accepted: Only common factors can be cancelled; x² is part of a sum, not a factor. Substituting x = 1 gives −4 in the original but −2.75 in Ronan's version.

scheme.for: a statement that only common factors cancel, and that x² is a term in a sum rather than a factor
supporting evidence: factorising first, or substituting a value to show the two expressions differ

hints: Compare with numbers: does $\dfrac{2 + 3}{2 + 4}$ simplify to $\dfrac{3}{4}$?
Try substituting $x = 1$ into both expressions.
What has to be true of something before it can be cancelled?
parts.workedSolution:
Cancelling divides the **whole** top and the **whole** bottom by the same thing, so only a common factor may go. Here $x^2$ is one term of a sum, not a factor of $x^2 + 5x + 6$.
A quick test settles it: at $x = 1$ the original is $\dfrac{1 + 5 + 6}{1 - 4} = \dfrac{12}{-3} = -4$, while Ronan's version gives $\dfrac{11}{-4} = -2.75$. The two are different expressions.

commonErrors.feedback: It is the single most reported error on this topic. Compare with numbers: $\dfrac{2+3}{2+4}$ is $\dfrac{5}{6}$, not $\dfrac{3}{4}$.

hints: Two numbers multiplying to 6 and adding to 5.
The bottom is a difference of two squares.
$(x + 2)$ is the common bracket.

commonErrors.feedback: Those solve $x^2 + 5x + 6 = 0$, which was not asked. 'Simplify' wants a tidier expression, never a value.

questions.solutionProgram: (x^2+5x+6)/(x^2-4) = (x+2)(x+3)/((x+2)(x-2)) = (x+3)/(x-2), checked at x = 1, 5.5, -1.5; cancelling the x^2 terms would give (5x+6)/(-4), which disagrees at x = 1 (11/-4 = -2.75 vs -4)

parts.stem:
A rectangle has area $(x^2 + 7x + 10)$ square units.

Show that the area can be written as $(x + 2)(x + 5)$.

(x + 2)(x + 5) reached, or the product expanded back to the printed quadratic

hints: A 'show that' may be finished either way, but the chain has to be visible.
parts.workedSolution: $2 \times 5 = 10$ and $2 + 5 = 7$, so $x^2 + 7x + 10 = (x + 2)(x + 5)$. Expanding back gives $x^2 + 5x + 2x + 10 = x^2 + 7x + 10$, as required.

commonErrors.feedback: The product is 10 but the sum is 11, not 7. Both conditions must hold; multiply back to check.

parts.stem:
The width of the rectangle is $\dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x + 5}$ units.

Find an expression for the length, simplified as far as possible.
hints: Length is area divided by width.
Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.
$x^2 - 4$ is a difference of two squares.
$(x + 2)$ cancels; the two $(x + 5)$ brackets multiply together.

commonErrors.feedback: The reciprocal was used, which earns two marks, but $x^2 - 4$ was left as a sum. Factorising it is what lets the $(x + 2)$ cancel.
One $(x + 5)$ was cancelled against nothing. There is an $(x + 5)$ in the area and another from the flipped width, so the answer carries $(x + 5)^2$.

findTheMistake.stem: Eimear was asked to simplify $\dfrac{x^2 - 4}{x^2 + 6x + 8}$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The $x^2$ terms are parts of sums, not factors. Cancelling divides the **whole** top and the **whole** bottom by the same thing, so only a common factor may be removed — and that means factorising first.
findTheMistake.feedback: Everything after line 1 is done carefully, but it is careful work on the wrong expression, so no marks are available. A ten-second test would have caught it: at $x = 1$ the original is $\dfrac{-3}{15} = -0.2$ and Eimear's version is $\dfrac{-2}{7} \approx -0.29$. November 2024 M4 Q19 named this directly: weaker candidates cancelled single terms across the fraction. Nothing may be crossed out until both parts are products.

findTheMistake.stem: Odhrán was asked to simplify $\dfrac{x^2 - 25}{x + 2} \div \dfrac{x - 5}{3x + 6}$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The division was turned into a multiplication correctly, and then the work stopped. Nothing was factorised, so nothing cancelled: $x^2 - 25 = (x + 5)(x - 5)$ and $3x + 6 = 3(x + 2)$, and both of those brackets have a partner below.
findTheMistake.feedback: Inverting the second fraction is the right first move and earns the method mark, which is exactly where November 2025 M4 Q22 reported most candidates stopping — only one in twenty finished. The habit to build is a fixed order: flip, then factorise **every** top and bottom, then cancel whole brackets, then write what is left. Two of those four steps were missing here, and each is a mark.

findTheMistake.stem: Tomás was asked to simplify $\dfrac{36 - y^2}{y^2 - 4y - 12}$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: $(y + 6)(y - 6)$ is $y^2 - 36$, not $36 - y^2$. The two differ by a factor of $-1$, so the whole answer comes out with the wrong sign.
correction: 36 − y² = (6 + y)(6 − y), keeping the order given
(6 − y) = −(y − 6), so the top is −(6 + y)(y − 6)
findTheMistake.feedback: The bottom is factorised correctly and the cancelling is carried out neatly, so an accuracy mark is realistic. The sign is what goes. Summer 2025 M4 Q20 reported exactly this: the difference of two squares went wrong when the letter was not the first term, because candidates swapped the terms round. Whatever starts the expression starts both brackets, and if the reversed bracket is needed, pull out the $-1$ deliberately.

prompts.prompt: What must be true before anything in an algebraic fraction can be cancelled?
prompts.answer: Both the top and the bottom must be written as products. Only a whole common factor cancels; a term inside a sum never does.

prompts.prompt: Why can you not cancel the $x^2$ in $\dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 + 7x + 12}$?
prompts.answer: Because $x^2$ is one term of a sum, not a factor of the whole expression. Compare with numbers: $\dfrac{2+3}{2+4}$ is $\dfrac{5}{6}$, not $\dfrac{3}{4}$.
$\dfrac{ac}{bd}$, and $\dfrac{a}{b} \times \dfrac{d}{c}$ — it is the **second** fraction that is turned over.

prompts.prompt: The four steps for dividing algebraic fractions.
prompts.answer: 1 Flip the second fraction and multiply. 2 Factorise every top and every bottom. 3 Cancel whole brackets. 4 Write the single fraction that is left.

prompts.prompt: Which factorising tools do you need on this topic?
prompts.answer: A common factor, the difference of two squares, a quadratic $x^2 + bx + c$, and grouping when there are four terms.
$\dfrac{x^2}{x} = x$: dividing powers of the same letter subtracts the indices. The numbers cancel separately, so the answer is $\dfrac{3x}{4}$.

prompts.prompt: You have simplified an algebraic fraction. What must the answer NOT contain?
prompts.answer: An equals sign, and no value of $x$. 'Simplify' asks for a tidier expression; solving is a different question.

prompts.prompt: $(5 - w)$ and $(w - 5)$ — how are they related, and how do you use it?
prompts.answer: $(5 - w) = -(w - 5)$. Pull the $-1$ out so the two brackets match, cancel them, and leave the minus sign in front of the fraction.
Group the top: $a(b + 3) + 2(b + 3) = (a + 2)(b + 3)$. The bottom is $(b + 3)(b - 3)$, so the answer is $\dfrac{a + 2}{b - 3}$.

prompts.prompt: Which algebraic-fraction questions belong to M4, not here?
prompts.answer: Adding or subtracting fractions whose denominators contain the unknown, such as $\dfrac{2}{x+2} + \dfrac{3}{2x-1}$. This statement covers simplifying, multiplying and dividing only.

findings.asked: Factorise the numerator and denominator of an algebraic fraction and simplify.
findings.wentWrong: About a third got full marks. Most took the common factor 2 out (some just divided by 2 instead), then partial credit for a difference of two squares. Weaker candidates cancelled single terms across the fraction or tried to solve it as an equation.
findings.rule: Only common factors cancel; an expression is simplified, never solved.

findings.asked: Factorise (grouping in the numerator, difference of two squares in the denominator) and cancel.
findings.wentWrong: Most got a mark for taking 3 out of the denominator. The difference of two squares went wrong when the letter was not the first term, because candidates swapped the terms round; grouping in the numerator troubled the less able.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the terms in their given order, wrote a squared minus b squared as (a + b)(a - b), and cancelled whole brackets.
findings.rule: 25 - w squared factorises as (5 + w)(5 - w) - do not reorder.

findings.asked: Divide one algebraic fraction by another and simplify.
findings.wentWrong: Only one in twenty finished. Most earned a mark or two for inverting the second fraction and factorising the denominators, then stalled.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Inverted, factorised every numerator and denominator, cancelled the common brackets, and wrote the single remaining fraction.
findings.rule: Flip, factorise everything, cancel whole brackets.

insight.ruleToRemember: Factorise every numerator and denominator first (HCF, difference of two squares, grouping), invert the second fraction when dividing, and cancel only whole matching brackets.
insight.aStarSignal: A division that needs three different factorising techniques before anything cancels, finished as one fraction in lowest terms.
